h1:
Chachoengsao Piah
& Old Thai Sweets of Paet Riu
intro: Mention souvenirs from Paet Riu (the old nickname for Chachoengsao) and most people think of piah — the Chinese-style filled pastry — before anything else. Chachoengsao has several old piah shops now run by the third generation, plus a handful of old Thai sweets that are hard to find in the big cities. We've picked the shops that are genuinely open right now, with rough prices and where to stop.

blocks.html: Chachoengsao is just over an hour from Bangkok, and plenty of people drive out to make merit at Wat Sothon and grab souvenirs on the way home. The most famous thing to take back is piah, which traces its roots to the old Chinese communities along the Bang Pakong River — both in town and out in Bang Khla district. Each shop has its own filling recipe and its own idea of how thin the pastry should be. We've ordered them by reputation and how easy they are to drop into.

blocks.text: Piah and souvenir shops worth a stop

items.name: Tang Seng Jua
items.blurb: One of the oldest piah shops in Paet Riu, baking and selling out the front of the house since around 1932 and now in its third generation. The signatures are the big mung-bean-and-salted-egg piah — thin pastry, packed filling — and a pork-floss piah tuned to Thai tastes. There are now several branches across the province, in town, Ban Pho, and Bang Khla, and a few of them double as a sit-down souvenir cafe.
items.meta: Local favourite · piah from about ฿20–35 each

items.name: Ueng Muy Seng (Bang Khla)
items.blurb: The legendary Bang Khla piah shop that has been part of the market for over a hundred years. It's known for big old-style piah with the traditional salted mung-bean filling and the mung-bean, winter-melon and salted-egg combination. Beyond piah, there are minced-pork-and-salted-egg steamed buns at around 20 baht each if you need something to tide you over. The shop sits across from Bang Khla fresh market, with roadside parking out front.
items.meta: Bang Khla · piah + buns, easy on the wallet

items.name: Rin Thai Sweets
items.blurb: A Thai-sweet shop in Paet Riu going back more than 50 years, making palace-style and old-fashioned sweets — thong yip, thong yot, foi thong, met khanun, khanom chan, khanom mo kaeng, and dok lamduan. A good pick for a gift box for an event or for taking back to older relatives.

items.name: Piah at Ban Mai Market
items.blurb: Inside the 100-Year Ban Mai Market there are several stalls selling piah and old Thai sweets — Bang Khla-style mung-bean-and-salted-egg piah, khanom tan (palm cake), and khanom bai bua. You can buy a single piece to taste before committing to a big bag, which makes it ideal if you want to sample several makers in one spot.
items.meta: Inside Ban Mai Market · open Sat–Sun/holidays

items.name: Jao Maphrao Kaeo (candied young coconut)
items.blurb: A local sweet made from young coconut sprout simmered until clear — fragrant with coconut and pleasantly chewy. It's a souvenir Paet Riu locals buy a lot, sold at souvenir shops in town and at Ban Mai Market, and it boxes up easily to carry.
items.meta: Local sweet · easy to carry home

items.name: Dried mango & mango products
items.blurb: Chachoengsao is nam dok mai mango country, so the souvenirs that follow are dried mango, candied mango, and oven-dried mango, sold at souvenir shops and mango orchards. There's the widest choice during mango season, roughly March to May.
items.meta: Straight from the orchard · mango season Mar–May

blocks.title: How to choose your piah
blocks.html: Thin-pastry, packed-filling piah keeps for less time than the thick-pastry kind. If you're buying it as a gift for someone in another province, ask the shop for the use-by date first, and go for the mung-bean-and-salted-egg filling, which lasts longer than the pork-floss kind.

blocks.text: 100-Year Ban Mai Market — eating old sweets by the river

blocks.html: If you'd rather wander and taste several old Thai sweets in one place, the 100-Year Ban Mai Market on the Bang Pakong River is where to go. It's an old timber market that has been trading since the reign of King Rama V, still holding onto its wooden shophouses, old-fashioned coffee stalls, and Chinese-Thai street food. The draw is the long run of food — savoury and sweet — lining the whole walkway.

items: Kuay teow pak mo (steamed rice-skin noodle rolls) — the market's signature: thin, soft skins wrapped around a packed filling, eaten hot as a light bite before you start on the sweets
Khanom tan & khanom bai bua — steamed Thai sweets scented with pandan and palm, hard to find in the big cities; buy them one at a time to taste
Bang Khla piah — several stalls in the market selling mung-bean-and-salted-egg piah to choose from
Old-style coffee — traditional sock-brewed coffee, strong and sweet, sipped by the river for the atmosphere

blocks.title: Market opening times
blocks.html: The 100-Year Ban Mai Market is open only on Saturdays, Sundays, and public holidays, roughly 08:00–16:30. On weekdays most stalls are shut, so if you're coming specifically to walk the market, plan it for a weekend or holiday.

blocks.text: Old Thai sweets worth trying at least once

blocks.html: Beyond piah, Chachoengsao has held onto plenty of old Thai sweets that have been made the same way since grandma's day. Many are made fresh and sell out by the day, so if you like traditional sweets, don't skip them.

items.name: Khanom mo kaeng (baked custard)
items.blurb: A soft Thai sweet with a fragrant browned top, made from egg, flour, and coconut milk. You'll find it at Thai-sweet shops in town like Rin Thai Sweets, and you can buy a whole tray to give as a gift.

items.name: Thong yip, thong yot & foi thong
items.blurb: The egg-based palace sweets in golden yellow, perfect as a gift for an auspicious occasion. The old Thai-sweet shops in town make them up as sets.

items.name: Khanom chan & dok lamduan
items.blurb: Chewy, pandan-scented layered khanom chan alongside dok lamduan flavoured with scented candle — old-style sweets that younger generations find harder and harder to come by.

blocks.text: How to shop for Paet Riu souvenirs and get your money's worth

items: Short on time? Just drop into a piah shop branch in town near Wat Sothon — easy to buy and easy to park.
If you want the atmosphere and the chance to taste several makers, set aside time for the 100-Year Ban Mai Market on a weekend.
For genuine Bang Khla-recipe piah, drive on out to Bang Khla district and stop at an originator like Ueng Muy Seng or the Bang Khla branch of one of the big names.
Fresh items like khanom mo kaeng and kuay teow pak mo are best eaten the same day, while piah and dried mango keep longer and travel better over a long distance.

faq.q: Which Chachoengsao piah shop is the most famous?
faq.a: The one most people think of first is Tang Seng Jua, an old shop in town that has been baking and selling since around 1932, plus Ueng Muy Seng out in Bang Khla district, which has been a Bang Khla piah legend for over a hundred years. Both are known for big mung-bean-and-salted-egg piah.

faq.q: How much does Paet Riu piah cost?
faq.a: Big piah run about 20–35 THB each depending on the filling and the shop, while the minced-pork-and-salted-egg steamed buns sold alongside them are around 20 THB each. Prices can shift over time, so it's worth checking again at the shop.

faq.q: What days is the 100-Year Ban Mai Market open?
faq.a: It's open only on Saturdays, Sundays, and public holidays, roughly 08:00–16:30. On weekdays most stalls are shut, so if you want to walk the old riverside market and taste the old-style sweets, come on a weekend or holiday.

faq.q: What old Thai sweets does Paet Riu have?
faq.a: There's khanom mo kaeng, khanom chan, dok lamduan, khanom tan, khanom bai bua, the egg-based sweets like thong yip, thong yot, and foi thong, and jao maphrao kaeo (candied young coconut), a local sweet. You'll find them at the old Thai-sweet shops in town and at Ban Mai Market.

faq.q: How long does a Paet Riu souvenir run take?
faq.a: If you only stop at a piah shop in town, it takes under an hour. But if you want to walk Ban Mai Market and drive out to Bang Khla too, allow half a day to a full day to do it comfortably — which pairs nicely with making merit at Wat Sothon.
